newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Cape/Panamax rates to fall, Handy rates promising.
newsitem.headline: Cape/Panamax rates to fall, Handy rates promising.

text.p: The managing director of Precious Shipping Plc (PSL) said on Thursday freight rates for Cape and Panamax vessels will continue falling this year while rates for Handy sized vessels will recover in 1997.

Khalid Hashim told the 5th International Bulk Congress in Singapore that supply of Cape and Panamax ships has been growing annually by 5.0 percent at a time when demand for the ships is rising by only 3.0 percent annually.
Earnings which used to average US$35,000 a day for Cape and Panamax vessels shipping ore or coal from the U.S. to Japan in 1995 have dropped to $12,000 a day in 1996 for the same route, he said.
"The small Handy sector shows the greatest promise. We strongly believe that the supply-demand imbalance in this sector is only set to grow," Hashim said.
Handymax and small Handy sized ships are common in the developing world and can ship cargo of up to 25,000 dwt. It is popular in the shipment of grains like rice, corn, soybeans or wheat.
But their number has been shrinking while demand for their services is growing steadily.
Precious Shipping has one of the biggest fleets of Handy-sized vessels in the world at 36 and has plans to buy more of the ships.
With demand growing, revenue from Handymax and Handy-sized ships should increase, Hashim said. Earnings for 1996 would range between $6,500-$6,900 a day against $7,100 a day in 1995.
"We feel that PSL would have earning figures similar to 1995 during 1997 and the years that follow could see dramatic jumps in earnings," he said.
Hashim said rates for Cape and Panamax vessels should recover as more ships become candidates for the scrapyard.
"We expect scrapping rates in 1996 to reach new records with the balance between supply and demand returning to this sector as early as 1997," he said.

Cape-sized vessels carry only iron ore and coal weighing over 100,000 dwt (deadweight tonnes) are the giants of the dry cargo trade. They transit through the Cape of Good Hope and are too large to sail through either the Suez or Panama canal.

Panamax ships carry grain along with iron ore and coal. They are the maximum size of ships that can steam through the Suez and the Panama canal, from which they get their name. Cargo can exceed 50,000 dwt.
